extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school students (Year 12 / IMO-level) seeking a first accessible account of the proof(s) of Fermat's Last Theorem
extracted.subtask_description: An expository guide aimed at advanced high-school students that collects definitions, statements, timelines and outlines of the proofs of Fermat's Last Theorem (Wiles' 1995 proof and later simplifications), with preliminaries and appendices to make the material approachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target perspective / audience
rubrics_metrics.description: We take the perspective of an advanced high school student trying to understand the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem for the first time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article is explicitly written to be 'beginner friendly' for this audience; the authors emphasise honest, student-level exposition (they are Year 12 / recent IMO participants). Expect motivation, preview of future learning, and simpler explanations rather than professional-level detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect necessary definitions and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: We collect definitions and statements needed to summarise how Fermat’s Last Theorem was first proved in 1995 as well as to see how the argument has simplified since then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all core definitions and theorems that a reader needs to follow the proof outline: Frey’s curve, discriminant, conductor, semistability, modular forms (weight/level), Galois representations, Ribet’s theorem, Wiles’ theorem, Serre’s conjecture, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner-friendly organisation and learning order
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise the content in a way that is beginner friendly, offering a preview of what students may expect to learn more deeply in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present material in a chronological/educational order: timeline → outline → preliminaries → main sections (Elliptic curves, Modular forms, Galois representations) → appendices. 'We try to spread [preliminaries] out as needed rather than all in one place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume prior mastery of proofs; replace full proofs by clarifications when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not claim to understand the proofs of the main statements and in fact we replace the proof environment that usually follows them by further clarifications of the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full technical proofs are out of scope for the intended audience, instead provide clarifications, explanations of terms used in the statements, intuitive sketches, and pointers to full proofs (appendices/references). Selectively explain proofs to match the authors' comprehension level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a clear timeline of historical and technical milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: We include a current timeline, outlines of proofs, background material and recent developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List classical contributions (n=3,4, Kummer, etc.), milestones leading to Wiles (TSW, Frey, Serre, Ribet), Wiles' work and gap/repair, and later updates (Modularity Theorem, Khare–Wintenberger, modern formalisation efforts). Provide dates and attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an initial high-level outline of the proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: We will first give an outline of the structure of the first proof of FLT without elaborating on the term Modular nor mentioning Galois Representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the main logical steps plainly (elementary base cases n=3,4; assume counterexample → Frey curve; Ribet: Frey curve not modular; Wiles: semistable curves modular → contradiction). Offer this outline before diving into technical machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present base cases and place elementary proofs in appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: We will need the n = 3, 4 cases for Wiles’ proof and their proofs are in our Appendix (12.1 and 12.1.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include elementary/accessible proofs (n=2,3,4) in appendices so that the main narrative can assume those base cases while keeping the main flow readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide thorough preliminaries tailored to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary sections introduce standard content that you might find in undergraduate courses that we do not assume the reader has completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover Abstract Algebra (groups, rings, fields, modules), Linear Algebra, Complex Analysis, Topology, Galois Theory, Representation Theory in the amounts needed for later sections. Spread preliminaries into the main text where immediately required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat some advanced terms as black boxes at first
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not assume the reader is familiar with the following key terms and treat them as black boxes for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing heavily technical objects (e.g., modularity, Galois representations), initially present their role and consequences without full formal development, deferring full definitions and technicalities to later sections or appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Frey’s curve and explain its key properties (discriminant, reduction, semistability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frey’s curve is defined from the equation y^2 = x(x − a^P)(x + b^P); include discriminant, good/bad/additive/multiplicative reduction, and the semistability property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show Frey’s curve is non-singular (∆ ≠ 0), compute ∆ = (abc)^{2P}, explain reduction modulo primes, define conductor N (for semistable curves N = product of primes of bad reduction) and prove for Frey curve N = rad(abc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the role and definition of modular forms (conductor/level, weight, Fourier expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word modular refers to the ability to associate a modular form: form f(z)=∑_n A_n e^{2πinz} on the upper half-plane H; define cusp form, periodicity, and the transformation rule with weight k and level N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State convergence region (Im z > 0), A_0 = 0 for cusp forms, periodicity f(z+1)=f(z), and the transformation condition f((az+b)/(cz+d))=(cz+d)^k f(z) for matrices with c ≡ 0 (mod N). Explain how the An sequence from point counts gives the q-expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Ribet’s level-lowering and the contradiction via nonexistence of level 2 weight 2 cusp forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribet showed that starting from the modular form of level N (the conductor) one can iteratively lower the level to obtain a non-zero cusp form of level 2 and weight 2; no such form exists, yielding a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the mechanism (if p | N but p^2 ∤ N, lower level by p; use Mazur to remove P if needed), explain why Frey’s curve has squarefree (hence reducible) conductor so the process ends at N=2 or N=2P, and cite the non-existence theorem for S2(Γ0(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce Galois representations coming from elliptic curves (torsion points, mod l and l-adic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galois representations arise from the action of Gal(¯Q/Q) on torsion points E[m] of an elliptic curve; looking at all powers of l gives l-adic representations, and at l-torsion gives mod l representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define m-torsion E[m], explain how Galois acts on these finite sets producing representations into GL2(F_l) (or GL2(Z_l) for l-adic), and outline how modularity statements apply to these representations (Serre's conjecture, epsilon conjecture).

rubrics_metrics.name: State and collect key theorems upfront to set learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Here are some examples of the theorems in the actual papers whose statements we hope to understand. We put some here upfront to set our goals for which definitions to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the key results (Ribet's theorem: TSW ⇒ FLT via Frey curve; Wiles' theorem: semistable elliptic curves over Q are modular; Serre's modularity conjecture and its consequences) with enough context so readers know what the end targets are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use worked propositions and short proofs to build intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Include propositions with proofs (e.g., Frey curve is non-singular and semistable; conductor N = rad(abc); formulae for Ap etc.) to illustrate definitions and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small propositions and explicit computations (discriminant computation, reduction behaviour, point counts modulo p, recurrence for A_{p^k}) as concrete anchors before abstract generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place specialised or lengthy technical material in appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that take us too far afield from the main discussion in terms of length or prerequisites are explored in the Appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices contain the base-case proofs, more advanced technical constructions (explicit conductor definition for non-semistable curves), expansions, and background material that would distract the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an honest, motivational pedagogical tone
rubrics_metrics.description: We are certainly not experts in any of these topics and will not try to hide our ignorance. ... To begin to understand FLT one mustn’t be a hostage to being logically prepared but also needs the right mix of motivation, hope and encouragement throughout their preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person student perspective, give encouragement, be explicit about what is deferred, and include acknowledgements and personal context to keep reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide references and multimedia resources for further study
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete achievements include producing over 100 pages of written material, alongside a collection of video recordings and supporting references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a bibliography (textbooks, original papers, expository books) and curated playlists/links to lectures or courses to enable deeper study (e.g., Stein, Silverman, Wiles, Serre, Khare–Wintenberger, YouTube playlists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show applied/computational checks and formulas (examples: dimension formula for S2(Γ0(N)))
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute and check specific formulas in examples (e.g., compute dim S2(Γ0(2)) using the dimension formula from Stein and verify it equals 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit evaluations in sample cases to demonstrate how abstract dimension/formulae translate to concrete nonexistence results used in the proof strategy.
